title: The Great Wall of China Episode
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the Great Wall of China: its disputed length (surveyed at roughly 13,000 miles / 21,000 km in 2007 versus the old 5,000 km estimate and the "ten thousand li" name), its construction over two thousand years by multiple dynasties with the Ming dynasty building most of it, forced labor by soldiers, commoners and criminals, guard towers and smoke/fire signaling, the Ming-era guard posts named for families, and the Qing-era decline. They debunk the myth, popularized by Robert Ripley, that the wall is visible from space or the Moon. They cover erosion from brick theft, grazing, firewood cutting, tourism, souvenir carving, roads and construction, desertification from the Gobi, and the government's later preservation efforts and laws with fines. Christen Conger, of the podcast Stuff Mom Never Told You, then describes her December visit near Beijing, including the steep climb, piped-in music, and a marriage proposal on the wall. A listener email about the podcast helping during recovery from depression closes the episode.
topics: Great Wall visible from space myth

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about Red Dawn, Wolverines and other small talk before turning to the Great Wall of China.

segments.title: Length of the Great Wall
segments.summary: The hosts explain the 'ten thousand li' name, li as a unit of measure, the long-held underestimates of the wall's length, and the 2007 Chinese survey that found it far longer, with the wall spanning a territory of about 20,000 kilometers in total and being a series of overlapping walls, trenches and natural barriers.

segments.title: Scholarship and neglect of the wall
segments.summary: China long viewed the wall as a relic of a backward feudal era. Brook Larmer's Smithsonian article is cited on the lack of scholarship, and changing attitudes after Deng Xiaoping called for preservation. Local repairs were sometimes poor, such as bathroom tiles used in one section.

segments.title: Robert Ripley and the space myth
segments.summary: The hosts debunk the claim that the Great Wall is visible from space or the Moon, which was popularized by Robert Ripley. Astronauts from low Earth orbit could sometimes see it under certain conditions, and a Chinese astronaut in 2003 reportedly confirmed it could not be seen.

segments.title: Construction history and the Huns
segments.summary: The wall was built in pieces from around 206 BC through many dynasties, with the Qin unifier Emperor Qin Shi Huang (called Chi in the transcript) linking earlier walls to keep out the Huns, who were skilled horse riders and archers. Soldiers, commoners and criminals built it, and criminals were sentenced to guard it by day and build it by night.

segments.title: Ming dynasty construction
segments.summary: The Ming dynasty built most of the wall, making it higher and wider, adding guard towers, bunkers and a smoke-and-fire signaling system. Guard posts were named after families who manned them, and the wall fell in the seventeenth century when the Manchu invaded, after which construction stopped.

segments.title: Qing neglect, Mao, and erosion
segments.summary: After the Qing took power the wall was viewed with scorn. Under Mao, people were encouraged to take bricks for building. Erosion also came from grazing cattle, freeze-thaw cycles, and firewood cutting that loosened soil beneath the wall.

segments.title: Desertification, tourism and modern threats
segments.summary: Desertification from the Gobi Desert, caused by historic deforestation and clearing near the wall, threatens sections. Tourists take bricks and carve graffiti, and souvenir shops, cable cars, roads and factories are built along or on the wall. The hosts discuss a rave held on the wall.

segments.title: Preservation laws and fines
segments.summary: China began taking preservation seriously, with provincial and then national laws banning brick removal, building close to the wall, and some harmful activities. Fines are described, and the hosts note enforcement is hard across the vast wall.

segments.title: Christen Conger's visit to the Great Wall
segments.summary: Christen Conger of Stuff Mom Never Told You describes her December trip to the wall near Beijing: a steep, windy climb, piped-in traditional music, crowds of Chinese tourists, and a marriage proposal at the highest lookout point.

segments.title: Listener mail on recovery
segments.summary: A listener thanks the show for helping during recovery from depression, saying listening during long runs helped them refocus on their passions and finish a degree in animation.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and point to social media, email and the website, and suggest searching the topic on the HowStuffWorks site.
